claims.text: The proposed method integrates machine learning with density functional theory.
Integrating machine learning with density functional theory can substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties for high-entropy systems.
The target domain includes elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The target systems include both solid and fluid states near phase transitions.
The method will predict free energies and entropy terms.
The intended conditions are high temperatures near phase transitions.
Local lattice distortion and dislocation motion mediate the proposed thermodynamic prediction method.
Machine-learning algorithms can learn patterns from density-functional-theory calculations to predict free energies and entropy terms.
Machine-learning prediction will reduce the need for costly molecular-dynamics simulations.
The method will reduce computational cost by at least 50% relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD.
The method will maintain at least 90% accuracy relative to experimental values.
The claimed applicability boundary extends to high-entropy systems containing up to 10 components.
The claimed temperature boundary is 500 K to 2000 K.
Model accuracy may depend on the quality and quantity of training data.
Model accuracy may depend on the selected density-functional-theory exchange-correlation functional.
The benchmark will compare predicted free energies, entropy terms, and computational cost with experimental values and the computational baseline.
Deviation from experimental values by more than 10% will falsify the hypothesis.
A computational-cost reduction of less than 30% relative to baseline will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires at least a 50% cost reduction, but the hypothesis is only falsified when the reduction is below 30%. Results between 30% and 50% would fail the stated prediction without falsifying the hypothesis.
